title: Elizaveta P. Sheremet
text:
Lay Perceptions of Science

I use quantitative methods, predominantly survey experiments, to examine how people evaluate scientific information. In particular, I study how non-scientists judge which scientific claims are plausible, and how institutional cues influence that judgments. ::: {style=“font-size: 95%; color: pink”} 1. Laypeople Use Institutional Information Cues in Judging the Plausibility of Research Findings
2025, Socius
with I. Deviatko, V. Polyakova, K. Fursov
 Print·  OSF *·
<details>

<summary> *Abstract*

</summary>

[Mediatization of science communication facilitates broader access
to scientific knowledge. However, in the post-truth era, it makes
the task of critical evaluation of science-based information more
challenging than ever for laypeople. The authors conducted a
factorial survey as a part of a nationally representative Russian
survey panel to evaluate the influence of institutional information
cues on laypersons’ plausibility judgments. The findings indicate
that funding information and institutional affiliation influence how
the general public perceives the plausibility of scientific results.
The data obtained also show that research results from various
scientific disciplines are perceived differently in terms of their
plausibility.]{.abstract}

title: Elizaveta P. Sheremet
text:
I am a PhD student and Paul F. Lazarsfeld Fellow in Sociology at Columbia University.
My research centers on science, folk science, and morality. My previous work focused on how informational cues about research—such as institutional affiliation and funding—shape lay perceptions of the plausibility of scientific claims. My current research examines when and how moral reasoning emerges among scientists, how it is expressed, and what factors shape or reinforce it.
This year, I am co-coordinating the SKAT Workshop at Columbia.
Before coming to Columbia, I received a BA and MA in Sociology from the Higher School of Economics in Moscow.
